newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane cleanup under way in North Carolina.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane cleanup under way in North Carolina.

text.p: North Carolina residents began returning to soaked and battered homes on Sunday to face a huge cleanup job after Hurricane Fran.
Dozens lined up at hardware stores to buy chainsaws and other repair tools. Others, whose homes were destroyed, sought food at church-run kitchens.
Convoys of trucks streamed into the state to fix utility poles, replace hundreds of miles (kilometres) of downed power lines, repair roads and haul away fallen trees and debris.
The effort to clear the debris received a boost from the National Guard, state forestry and transportation departments, and prisoners.
Washington, however, was bracing itself for the fallout from Fran as rising floodwaters in the Potomac River threatened the nation's capital on Sunday.

After Fran dumped four inches (10 cm) of rain in the capital and up to 14 inches (35 cm) in outlying areas, forecasters predicted a flood surge of 13 to 15 feet (4-4.5 metres) in the wealthy Georgetown section of the city and up to 34 feet (10 metres) at Harpers Ferry, West Virginia.
Rising floodwaters also threatened to close the main road to National Airport, the city's domestic airport.
Hurricane Fran cut a swathe of destruction from Cape Fear on the southeastern end of North Carolina, where it came ashore, to the northwest of the state.

At least 15 people were killed in the state, including a firefighter and Marine, "and there may be more," Sara Kempin, a spokeswoman for North Carolina Emergency Management Centre, said. Some drowned and others were killed when trees fell on their cars or houses, she said.
Disaster declarations were made for 24 more counties in the state, mostly inland, bringing the total to 34.

"The devastation is widespread across coastal and inland counties, and I want to do all we can to help rebuild North Carolina and help our people get their lives back together," Gov. Jim Hunt said in a statement.
There were 728,667 customers still without power throughout the state, and electric utility crews from Georgia, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee and West Virginia were on hand to help restore power.
All major railroads remain closed in the Carolinas pending restoration of signals, track repair and debris clearance. And 24 Red Cross shelters were open in North Carolina for 300 people.
In the port city of Wilmington, authorities said they were beginning to allow residents to return to Carolina Beach and Kure Beach, two seaside towns on Pleasure Island, off Wilmington.
They had been barred since Thursday because electric, water and sewer services were severed and many properties were still extremely unsafe, officials said.

A 24-hour curfew was in effect for both towns and a curfew from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. was imposed on the rest of New Hanover County. Authorities said schools would remain closed on Monday while damage was assessed.
Airspace over the beaches hardest hit by Fran has been closed, since sightseers were deemed to be posing a hazard to airborne disaster relief crews.

"A no-fly zone has been established from two miles offshore to two miles inland from the New River Inlet south to Holden Beach," William Dudley, state deputy secretary of Crime Control and Public Safety, said.
In Wrightsville Beach, a town on a barrier island off Wilmington, officials said safety concerns would keep residents from returning for at least three days.
On Topsail Island, north of Wilmington, rescue workers searched homes in North Topsail Beach for missing people.

"We're going house to house on the beach looking for people who might have been trapped. We're finding people -- they're scared. They were freaked out by the storm," Marian Kleinman, a spokeswoman for Onslow County, said.
An elderly woman who was found floating on a mattress in a marsh near Surf City after the storm was in critical condition, reports said. Her trailer home was destroyed.
As National Guard troops patrolled the islands, bulldozers scraped sand from beaches and roads. Diggers scooped chunks of crumbled houses and slabs of broken asphalt out of the way.
"Major roads have been cleared. Almost all the county and city roads are open," Bruce Shell, spokesman for Wilmington's New Hanover County, said.
The Wilmington City Council passed an emergency ordinance on Saturday to prevent price gouging, making it punishable by a $500 fine or 30 days in jail.
